item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports learning recommendation-specific text representations, but the retrieved 2024–2026 work does not establish an exact match for a randomly initialized text encoder jointly trained with GRU4Rec. [JEPA4Rec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10512) learns item representations from descriptive text using masked representation prediction and sequence-related objectives; its Transformer architecture and two-stage training differ from the required GRU setup. [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602) shows that pretrained text embeddings can be insufficiently discriminative. Its external embeddings and WhitenRec+ ensemble are unsuitable here; the relevant lesson is to measure representation quality rather than assume semantic similarity implies recommendation relevance.\n\nAn older, more direct architectural precedent is [Ask the GRU (2016)](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=1255): jointly optimized text representations plus item-specific residual embeddings, with supervised mean-word and GRU text encoders. However, its experiments used externally pretrained word embeddings, and its GRU encodes document text rather than interaction histories. A constraint-compatible hypothesis is therefore one GRU4Rec network whose item representation adds an ID embedding to a projected mean of randomly initialized title/description token embeddings, all trained through the recommendation loss. Shared tokens could transfer training signal to sparse items, while ID residuals capture behavior unexplained by text. This is an experimental adaptation, not a demonstrated gain on the four Amazon categories; assess it against the corrected baseline using fixed macro validation HR@10 and measured sparse-item behavior."}
